skill.name: privilege-escalation-knowledge
skill.description: Guides authorized Linux privilege escalation practice with enumeration steps, common misconfigurations, and post-exploitation verification in lab or CTF environments.
skill.summary: Structured Linux privilege escalation reference for authorized lab and training work.
skill.author: CharlesKozel

security_audit.summary: The skill is a Markdown privilege-escalation playbook, so Markdown fence detections were marked false positive while actionable escalation guidance was confirmed. Confirmed findings include root shell escapes, SUID modification, password file tampering, Docker socket escape, credential discovery, SSH persistence, and pipe-to-shell execution. Semantic review also found end-to-end root compromise intent, persistence guidance, credential harvesting, and root flag capture.

remediation.suggestion: Rewrite exploit steps as defensive checklists that explain risk, detection, and remediation without shell-escape commands or root-compromise procedures.
Remove instructions for SUID bash, root SSH key insertion, writable root-run scripts, and other persistence mechanisms.
Replace credential-search commands with defensive audit guidance focused on secret storage, file permissions, and rotation procedures.

remediation.issue: Remote script execution and exploit downloads
remediation.suggestion: Remove pipe-to-shell commands and kernel exploit transfer steps. Reference vetted lab resources only with explicit authorization warnings.
Add explicit scope requirements and limit all examples to toy lab scenarios or non-executable pseudocode.

semantic_findings.title: End-to-End Root Compromise Workflow
semantic_findings.description: The skill directs users from low privilege access to root, then to root flag capture. This is an offensive compromise workflow, even when framed for labs.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The purpose and decision tree explicitly describe escalating to root through sudo, SUID, capabilities, cron, linpeas, and kernel exploits.

semantic_findings.title: Persistence And Backdoor Guidance
semantic_findings.description: The skill recommends SUID bash and root SSH authorized keys as backup access after compromise. These are persistence mechanisms, not only verification steps.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The text says to maintain access after root and includes both SUID and root SSH key methods. The decision tree also names a backdoor path.

semantic_findings.title: Credential Harvesting Playbook
semantic_findings.description: The skill instructs searching web roots, system paths, shell histories, SSH keys, and application configs for credentials. This is credential harvesting guidance.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The section is titled credentials in files and lists multiple sensitive locations to search. The intent is clearly credential discovery during escalation.

semantic_findings.title: Root Flag Capture And Reporting
semantic_findings.description: The skill tells users to locate, read, save, and report root flags after privilege escalation. In non-lab settings, the same pattern is sensitive data capture.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The instructions explicitly require reading root-owned flag files and saving the result. The CTF framing reduces ambiguity but not the misuse risk.

content.value_statement: Linux privilege-escalation reviews require a structured checklist for authorized systems. This skill organizes enumeration, common vectors, and reporting steps for lab or internal security work.
actual_capabilities: Outlines a three-layer Linux privilege escalation workflow.
Lists manual checks for sudo, SUID, cron, capabilities, and writable files.
Summarizes common vectors such as sudo abuse, SUID binaries, Docker escape, and NFS misconfiguration.
Provides troubleshooting options for file transfer, write permissions, and missed vectors.
Defines success criteria for root access and flag collection in lab scenarios.
limitations: Does not verify authorization or engagement scope.
Contains offensive commands that can harm real systems if misused.
Does not replace current CVE validation or exploit reliability testing.
Assumes Linux lab targets and may not fit production hardening workflows.

use_cases.title: Structure Authorized Lab Practice
use_cases.description: Follow a repeatable order for privilege-escalation checks in a CTF or training target.

use_cases.title: Review Internal Linux Misconfigurations
use_cases.description: Map observed findings to common escalation paths during an approved internal assessment.

use_cases.title: Build A Defensive Checklist
use_cases.description: Convert offensive vectors into hardening tasks for sudo, SUID, cron, and credential exposure.

prompt_templates.title: Create A Beginner Checklist
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a safe privilege-escalation checklist for an authorized Linux training machine. Group checks by sudo, SUID, cron, capabilities, and credentials.

prompt_templates.title: Prioritize Lab Findings
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these enumeration notes from my authorized lab and rank likely privilege-escalation paths. Explain evidence and next validation steps without destructive actions.

prompt_templates.title: Convert To Remediation
prompt_templates.prompt: Turn this privilege-escalation method into a defender remediation plan with affected controls, detection ideas, and hardening steps.

prompt_templates.title: Draft An Advanced Report
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare a concise report for an authorized Linux lab compromise path. Include assumptions, evidence, risk, containment, and remediation priorities.

output_examples.input: I found a writable cron script in an authorized lab.
output_examples.output: Treat it as high risk. Explain who can edit it, which account runs it, expected execution timing, and how to remove unsafe write access.

output_examples.input: A SUID binary appears unusual on a Linux training target.
output_examples.output: Compare it to baseline system binaries, identify the owner and permissions, document why it matters, and propose removing unnecessary SUID permissions.

output_examples.input: I need a defensive summary after a lab privilege escalation.
output: State the verified path from low privilege to root.
List the misconfiguration that enabled the path.
Recommend least-privilege, file-permission, and monitoring fixes.

best_practices: Use only on systems where you have written authorization.
Convert each offensive path into a remediation or detection item.
Keep exploit testing isolated to disposable labs or approved test windows.
anti_patterns: Running examples on production or third-party systems.
Adding persistence mechanisms without explicit scope approval.
Treating flag capture as proof for real incident handling.

faq.question: Is this skill safe for automatic use?
faq.answer: No. It includes offensive escalation steps and should require human review before use.

faq.question: Who is the intended user?
faq.answer: Security learners, assessors, and administrators working inside authorized Linux lab or assessment environments.

faq.question: Does it run commands by itself?
faq.answer: No. It is a Markdown knowledge base, but it tells an agent or user which commands to run.

faq.question: Can defenders use it?
faq.answer: Yes. Defenders can map each attack path to hardening, monitoring, and access-control improvements.

faq.question: Does it validate legal authorization?
faq.answer: No. Users must confirm authorization, scope, and change-control requirements before applying any guidance.

faq.question: What is the main risk?
faq.answer: The skill can guide root compromise, credential discovery, persistence, and sensitive data capture if misused.
